interactive.title: Bars that become an area
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on bars under a rate graph. Each graph shows a rate against time, a current in amps or a speed in metres per second, drawn from a rule the screen names. Under it stand bars of equal width, each as tall as the rate at one moment, so each bar's area is a rate times a time: amps times seconds is coulombs of charge, and metres per second times seconds is metres. A running total adds the bars up. A slider sets how many bars share the same stretch of time, from 4 to 100, so the bars get thinner as their number grows. The first screen has a steady 3 A for 4 s, one rectangle, 3 × 4 = 12 C. Then the current i = 3t² amps from 0 s to 2 s. Each bar takes the current at its start, so on this rising curve every bar falls short of the curve by a thin sliver, and 4 bars give 5.25 C. More bars miss thinner slivers: 6.56 C at 8 bars, 7.88 C at 100, settling on 8 C. Beside it is the reverse rule from the last lesson: the charge is q = t³ + c, and its value at 2 s take away its value at 0 s, (8 + c) − (0 + c), is 8 C, the number the bars settle on, written ∫₀² 3t² dt. Steps climb its curve, each one bar's charge stacked on the last, so the bars' total is nearly the curve's whole rise. A later screen measures each bar's height at its middle instead: each bar's top then crosses the curve, poking above it on the bar's left half while the curve rises above it on the right half, and the two slivers nearly match, so 4 bars give 7.875 C. Where a current turns negative, flowing back, its graph dips below the axis; those bars hang below it, hatched, and count as minus in the total. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the graph.
interactive.ignores: The currents and speeds are example rules, chosen so the numbers come out exactly; a real current graph is usually measured, not given by a rule. A current rising as 3t² is not how a capacitor charges from a steady supply through a resistor, where the current is largest at the start and falls away. The reverse rule here is for powers of t; other rates, such as the sine waves of a.c., need reverses of their own, not shown.

explain.text:
Adding up a rate over a stretch of time gives the total it delivers: current added up over time is charge, and speed added up over time is distance. You can add it up with bars, and the reverse rule from the last lesson gets the bars' exact total in one subtraction.

When a speed holds steady, the distance is the speed times the time, the area of the rectangle under its flat graph.[^1] Any steady rate works the same way: a steady 3 A for 4 s moves 3 × 4 = 12 C, because an amp is a coulomb each second. When the rate changes, no single rectangle fits, so cut the time into narrow bars, take the rate as steady across each one, and add their amounts. That is what an integral is, a quantity described as a sum of many small pieces.[^2] Take a current that rises, i = 3t² amps, from 0 s to 2 s. Cut the 2 s into 4 bars, each 0.5 s wide, and give each bar the current at its start: 0, 0.75, 3 and 6.75 A. Each bar's charge is its current times 0.5 s, and together they make 5.25 C. That is short, because the current keeps rising across each bar while the bar's flat top does not, so each bar misses a thin sliver under the curve. Thinner bars miss thinner slivers: 8 bars give 6.56 C, 100 give 7.88 C, and the total settles on 8 C. Taking each bar's height at its middle gets close much sooner. The bar's top then crosses the curve: on the bar's left half it pokes above the curve, on its right half the curve rises above it, and the two slivers nearly cancel, so 4 bars give 7.875 C. On a straight line the two slivers are the same size, so mid-height bars give the exact total. Your MCA papers call this the [[mid-ordinate rule]]: the Applied Heat syllabus uses it to find the area of an indicator card, an engine's pressure–volume graph.[^3]

Now the reverse rule. Charge is what you get by integrating the current over the time,[^4] and the last lesson gives q = t³ + c. The charge that flows between 0 s and 2 s is the charge at the end take away the charge at the start: (8 + c) − (0 + c) = 8 C, the number the bars settle on. The c cancels, so any c will do.[^5] Here is why the two agree. Each thin bar is the current, how fast the charge grows, times a short time, so it is very nearly how much q rises across that bar. The rise across the first bar, plus the rise across the second, and so on, is the rise from start to end, because each bar picks up where the last left off. Thinner bars make each "very nearly" closer, so the bars' total settles on exactly that rise. So instead of adding bars, take the reverse rule's answer, call it F, put in the end time b and the start time a, and subtract: F(b) − F(a).[^6] Adding bars usually only approximates, unless the rate is steady or, with mid-heights, a straight line; the rule gets it at once.[^7] This is a [[definite integral]], an integral with two ends, written ∫₀² 3t² dt = 2³ − 0³ = 8, the small numbers on the ∫ being the start and end.

A current can flow back. Say i = 4 − 2t amps from 0 s to 3 s: it flows forwards until 2 s, then turns negative. A negative current times a time is a negative amount, charge taken away, so bars below the axis count as minus: 4 C forwards, then 1 C back, 3 C in all. Count the 1 C back as plus and you get 5 C, more than ever arrived. The reverse rule does the minus for you: F(t) = 4t − t² is 12 − 9 = 3 at 3 s and 0 at 0 s, so 3 C. A definite integral gives the change, and the new value is the starting value plus the integral of the rate.[^8] The capacitor from the last lesson held 3 C at 0 s with a current of t amps. The reverse rule turns t into 0.5t², so ∫₀⁴ t dt = 0.5 × 16 − 0 = 8, and it held 3 + 8 = 11 C at 4 s, as you found there. You will hear that the integral is the area under the curve, and it is, counting area below the axis as minus. But physics-education researchers found that students who could say so did not necessarily connect the area with the adding up, so they could not use it on new problems.[^9] Under a current graph the area's units are amps times seconds, coulombs: a charge. **Bars under a rate graph add up the amount, rate × time, bar by bar; as they thin, their total settles on F(b) − F(a), the reverse rule's value at the end minus its value at the start,[^7][^6] with bars below the axis counting as minus.**

analogy.text: Remember the kWh meter from the first lesson? Log a workshop's load every half hour and take each reading as the load for that half hour: each reading is a bar, kW × 0.5 h of energy, and the day's bars add up to its kWh. Log every few minutes and the total closes in on what the meter says, its evening reading take away its morning one. The meter's reading plays F, and its difference is the exact total the bars are closing in on.
analogy.breaks: The meter finds the day's total by measuring the energy as it flows, not from a rule. A rate given as a rule needs the reverse rule to find F; a log of readings has no rule to reverse, so adding up bars is all it allows.

practice.text:
- Check the units first: the rate times the time should give the amount you want (amps × seconds = coulombs, metres per second × seconds = metres).
- If you have the rate as a rule, integrate it term by term with the reverse rule. Leave out the c, because it cancels.
- Put in the end time, then the start time, and take the second from the first: F(b) − F(a).
- If you have only a graph, split the time into equal strips, read the rate at the middle of each strip, add those readings and multiply by the strip width: the mid-ordinate rule.[^3]
- Count parts below the axis as minus. That gives the net change. For the total either way, such as how far a boat went out and back, work out each part's size on its own and add the sizes.

**Rules of thumb:** more, thinner strips get closer. On a straight stretch a mid-height strip is exact. The answer is the change, so to find where the amount ends up, add it to the starting value.[^8]

**Worked example:** Say a current falls steadily, i = 8 − 2t amps, and you want the charge that flows from 1 s to 3 s. The reverse rule gives F(t) = 8t − t². At 3 s, F = 24 − 9 = 15; at 1 s, F = 8 − 1 = 7. The charge is 15 − 7 = 8 C. Check with one mid-height strip: at 2 s the current is 8 − 4 = 4 A, and 4 A × 2 s = 8 C, exact because the graph is straight.

**Where you will meet it:** an HN engineering maths unit applies integration to the area under a velocity time curve, giving distance travelled.[^10]

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the height as the amount: a current at one moment is not a charge.
- Adding the heights and forgetting to multiply by the width.
- Forgetting to take away F(a) when the start is not at 0.
- Putting the end times into the rate instead of its reverse rule.
- Taking the end from the start, F(a) − F(b), which flips the sign.
- Counting parts below the axis as plus when you want the net change.

interactive.html:
A rate graph, current or speed against time, with bars standing under it; above it, the running total of the bars.

Every rule is an example; every total is worked out from the rule drawn.
interactive.title: Bars that become an area
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the slivers between bars and curve shrinking as the running total settles on 8 C, what t³ gives from 0 s to 2 s, when you slide the bars from 4 to 100.

checks.label: When the speed or current is constant, the area under its flat graph is just the rate times the time: on both steady screens, bars of any number add up to exactly that, and the running total drawn shows it

An integral describes a quantity as a sum of many small pieces: on every screen with bars, each bar drawn stands for its height times its width, and the running total drawn is the sum of those pieces, those below the axis taken away

The charge can be determined by integrating the current over the time interval: under the rising current every extra bar raises the running total, which stays short of the reverse rule’s charge and closes in on it, as the bars screen draws

Any antiderivative works: with any number added to the reverse rule, its value at the end take away its value at the start is the same, so the rise drawn on the reverse-rule screen stays the same at every moment of its demonstration

Evaluating the antiderivative at the ends of the interval and subtracting: every reverse rule here, differentiated by its slope worked out from the rule, gives back the rate it came from, and each answer the puzzles accept by the reverse rule is its value at the end take away its value at the start

Adding the areas of rectangles only approximates, and the theorem is straightforward by comparison: bars at their starts under the rising current always fall short of the reverse rule’s answer, mid-height bars land far closer with the same number, and under a straight-line rate mid-height bars give it exactly

The new value equals the initial value plus the integral of the rate of change: the last lesson’s capacitor, holding a known charge at the start and fed a steadily rising current, ends with that charge plus what its current’s bars settle on

Integration applied to the area under a velocity time curve gives the distance travelled: on each speed screen the running total of the bars or of the area under the speed is the distance the puzzle accepts, in metres

Bars below the axis hang under it, hatched, and count as minus: on every screen where the current turns back, each bar under the axis is hatched with a negative amount, runs back along the running total’s lower lane, and the total drawn takes it away

Thinner bars miss thinner slivers: on the bars screen the slivers drawn add up to exactly what the running total misses and shrink as the bars thin; mid-height bars, the mid-ordinate rule, draw an extra and a missed sliver in each bar that nearly cancel, 0.125 C apart

From the rules, by hand: 3 A for 4 s is 12 C and 5 m/s for 6 s is 30 m; 3t² from 0 s to 2 s has start heights 0, 0.75, 3 and 6.75 A, 5.25 C from 4 bars, 6.56 C from 8, 7.88 C from 100, 8 C exactly; the bar from 1 s to 1.5 s is 3 A × 0.5 s = 1.5 C; 8 − 1 = 7 C from 1 s to 2 s, 12 − 3 = 9 the slip; 4 mid-height bars give 7.875 C, 0.125 C short; t² from 0 s to 6 s gives mid-heights 1, 9, 25 and 70 m, 72 m exactly; 4 − 2t gives 4 C forwards, 1 C back, 3 C net; 3 − t gives 4.5 C each way, 0 C net; 2t + 3 gives 28 − 4 = 24 m, 11 − 5 = 6 the slip; 2t − 4 gives 4 C back, 9 C forwards, 5 C net; and the screens’ words quote these values
Every puzzle offers three different answers and accepts only the right one; each answer’s number is the value its slip gives

Before Check no puzzle gives its verdict: nothing red, the working ends in a question mark and the total reads ?; a picked answer only marks its own value on the total; a right answer fills the total with nothing red; every wrong answer shows its slip in red
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, and every pick’s or answer’s motion within 1.3 s
